children.title: The gate page's scope paragraph never mentions the third channel, and a test pins the stale wording
children.body:
`frontend/src/app/gate/page.tsx:89-100` tells the reader there are two channels: orders placed through this tool ("a channel that has never carried one") and a bet placed in the Kalshi app ("fires no check before it happens"). Both are still literally true. But since 2026-08-26 there is a third and the paragraph does not name it: the in-portal hand bet, which DOES fire checks — `place_manual_order` (`backend/api/routes.py:4576`) runs twelve server-side checks including the desk lockout, the cool-off, the daily-loss switch over `venue_settlements`, balance-derived caps, a typed price ceiling, a depth check, and `MANUAL_ORDER_MAX_SPEND_TENTHS = 3_000` (`backend/store/manual_orders.py:104`).

The test is part of the problem rather than the guard against it: `tests/test_scope_sentences.py:58-66` pins the "fires no check" wording with the docstring "until the manual path (ADR 0063) ships a button". The button shipped — `ManualTicket` renders from the market page, /slate, LiveBoard, MarketSearch, ParlayCards and PriceOnKalshi. The test now protects a sentence written for a world that ended.

Second, smaller item in the same area: `backend/store/manual_orders.py:18-22` still says the constant "stays True until the C0 probe…", four lines above `MANUAL_ORDERS_ARE_DRY_RUNS = False` (:70). A docstring asserting the opposite of the line it documents is the exact failure mode CLAUDE.md names.

#9 deliberately did not touch either: the new Gate lede ("The bets you place by hand go through a different door with its own limits, and this lock never touches them") is true and complete on its own, and rewriting a test-pinned paragraph is a separate decision.

children.title: Nothing describes a tab before it is tapped, and nothing ever will
children.body:
Joe's words in #9 were "i havent the faintest clue what the other tabs are for", said about the nav. #9's answer is six page-top sentences, so the answer arrives one tap after the question.

That was decided on physics, not preference. `Nav.tsx:227` is an `overflow-x-auto` row already scrolling 424 into 318 at 390px with six bare words, so a subtitle under each pill pushes Gate and Your bets off the strip — the loss `Nav.tsx:96-98` exists to prevent. A `title=` tooltip is ruled out four separate times in this repo (`Term.tsx:6-7`, `HowToRead.tsx:5-10`, `Hint.tsx:7-14`, `slate/page.tsx:842-843`) because a phone has no hover, and `Hint.tsx`'s sanctioned tap-target pattern would put a tap target inside the nav row competing with navigation.

So the residual gap is structural, and the honest position is that it is small: nothing is ever bet from the nav strip, and the cost is one tap per tab, once. But nobody has checked that with Joe, and there is no onboarding, first-run, welcome or help surface anywhere in `frontend/src` (grepped: zero hits) — the app has never introduced itself to a new reader.

Questions to grill: does he want to know what a tab is before opening it, or was "what is this for" a question he only has once? Is the footer's "Also served" list — label plus blurb, rendered on every route (`app/layout.tsx:50-55`) — evidence that a pre-tap form works, or evidence that it works only for screens he rarely opens? Do NOT open this as a build; constraint 7 of #9 forbids new screens, and the answer may well be "nothing".

children.title: What colour the real-money warning strip wears once red is scarce
children.body:
Part of #3

## Question

Opened by the resolution of #10 (Brand red and loss red are the same colour), which chose Split A: `--accent` becomes indigo and means identity + commit; red is surrendered to loss; REJECTED moves to the warning ochre.

That leaves one red thing on the hand-bet path with no ruling on it. `ManualTicket.tsx:476` renders the real-money warning as:

```
border-accent/50 bg-accent-soft
```

which is **byte-identical to the REJECTED chip's treatment today** (`SlateRow.tsx:54`). Under Split A the chip goes ochre and the confirm button (`:563`) goes indigo, so the strip is left holding a red tint that now belongs to `--negative` alone. `TicketSheet` has the same shape at `:514` (`border-negative/50 bg-negative/10`, the confirm error).

**The prototype drew the strip red and that was an unreviewed call**, made to keep the specimen readable rather than because it was decided.

Settle which it is:

- **Red.** "This spends real money" is a danger message and red is now unambiguously the danger colour. Costs: the confirm button below it is indigo, so the warning and the action disagree in hue; and red was just made *rare* on purpose, so spending it here is spending the scarcity.
- **Ochre.** It is the same class of message as every other "do not trust this / be careful" string in the app, which is what `--accent-2` already carries. Costs: it then looks like a refusal notice sitting above a live buy button.
- **Indigo.** It belongs to the commit action it introduces. Costs: the one strip whose job is to slow him down would wear the colour of the button.
- **No tint at all** — foreground ink on the card, bordered. Costs: the anti-impulse structure loses its only visual weight.

Constraints this inherits and may not break: ADR 0073 and the map's own out-of-scope list forbid anything that removes the typed probability, the typed order token, or the ten-minute rest. This ticket changes a colour, not a control.

Use `/grilling`. The answer names what the strip *is* — a warning, a label on the action, or a brake — and the colour follows from that.

children.title: Which of the six components that refused colour now take it
children.body:
Part of #3

## Question

**This is the payoff of #10 and it is currently unowned.**

The resolution of #10 established that six components gave up an emphasis they wanted, in comments, rather than say *bad* — because `--accent` was byte-identical to `--negative`:

- `board/page.tsx:463` and `slate/page.tsx:920` — both `Stat` functions carry "No accent variant, deliberately", pinned by `tests/test_palette_contrast.py:81`
- `FairValueSteps.tsx:32` — "**No colour.** `--accent` is the same red as `--negative` in both themes, so a coloured margin bar would read as a verdict"
- `ParlayDifficulty.tsx:28` — "None. Every mark is an ink token… a coloured series here would read as a verdict on a number that is not one"
- `GoodChancePicks.tsx:28` — "No `bg-accent` (red = money), no urgency ink"
- `slate/page.tsx:216` — the parlay link takes "no accent — the desk's own screen carries the caveats"

Once `--accent` is indigo, the *stated reason* for four of those five refusals evaporates. **It does not follow that they take the colour**, and that is the decision: which of them was refusing colour because red meant loss, and which was refusing colour because **a mark on a chart is a claim** and the number does not support one?

`ParlayDifficulty` and `FairValueSteps` state the second reason as well as the first, so they may be unaffected. `GoodChancePicks` states a third — a favourites list must not become a chase surface — which #8's resolution reinforced with two new prohibitions and pinned in `tests/test_good_chance_picks.py`. `Stat` is the clearest case: its guard's premise becomes false, and #10 already ruled the replacement guard is "a count is a fact, not a verdict — no Stat wears `--negative`."

Answer per component, not in general. For each: does it take indigo, stay ink, or stay refused — and if it takes it, what is the *one* thing on that screen the colour is spent on.

**This is the ticket that decides whether the cockpit gets an identity or just stops being red.** It is also where "cool means all four levers at once" (the map's standing preference) meets the size-tier question in #17 — the two should be read together, and #17 is now blocked only by #16.

Use `/grilling` and `/domain-modeling`. Read #10's resolution first; the token values and every contrast ratio are settled there and are not reopened here.

children.title: Ochre became the body text: is the wash a defect or the true state?
children.body:
Part of #3

## The observation

Ten screenshots of the live Games screen on Joe's phone, 2026-08-28 04:38Z, on the ADR 0081 palette (live `bc256e3`). Every row carries **three separate ochre elements across four lines**:

```
soft fallback                                      <- --accent-2   (already was)
Books last read 198 min ago -- past the 15 min     <- --accent-2   (already was)
limit. Not actionable until the odds are refreshed.
stale_odds                                         <- --accent-2   (WAS RED)
the sportsbook lines had aged out -- needs a refresh   <- muted
READINGS DISAGREE BY 2.1 PTS -- tap for the ranges     <- muted
```

Repeated for all 100 rows on the slate. **Ochre has stopped reading as a warning and become the body text of the screen.**

ADR 0081 caused the third line. `stale_odds` — the machine-readable suppression code — was `--accent` red and moved to `--accent-2` ochre, correctly, because a refusal is not a loss. The rule is right and the screen got worse: the code was the one element visually separated from the human sentence above it, and it is now the same colour.

**And there is no indigo anywhere below the nav tile.** Across ten screenshots of the primary screen, the only brand colour is the 32px logo. #10's premise was that every emphasis read as "this is bad"; that is fixed, and nothing took over the emphasis, because the six components in #33 are still refusing colour. The screen went from *wrongly* emphasised to *not* emphasised.

## The question this ticket has to answer FIRST, before any repaint

**Is the wash a design defect, or the palette correctly reporting the state?**

At the moment of capture the books had not been read for **198 minutes**, `BETTABLE` was **0**, `ON THE SLATE` was **100**, and the refresh panel said no row on this instance has ever cleared the fee. Every row on that screen genuinely *is* stale, refused and unbettable. A screen where everything is refused arguably *should* look like a screen where everything is refused, and repainting it would be making a true screen lie.

**The measurement that separates them, and it costs 4 credits:** tap *Team lines, whole slate* (taps had used 0 of 150 for the day), then re-capture the same screen.

- If the ochre collapses to a handful of rows → the palette is honest, and the real defect is showing 100 dead rows at all. That is a filtering question (#15) and not a colour one, and this ticket closes pointing there.
- If the wash survives on fresh odds → it is a design defect and the rest of this ticket applies.

**Do not skip this step.** Every option below is a repaint, and repainting a screen that is accurately reporting a stale slate is the exact failure ADR 0071 §2.3 warns about: a per-row fact is transparency, and dressing it up is a claim.

## If it survives fresh odds — the actual decision

Which of the three ochre elements gives up the colour. They say overlapping things, which is the underlying content problem the palette merely exposed:

| element | says | note |
|---|---|---|
| `soft fallback` | the devig fell back to non-sharp books | a *different* fact from staleness |
| "Books last read 198 min ago…" | the odds aged out, in words | the human sentence |
| `stale_odds` | the odds aged out, as a code | **says the same thing as the line above it** |

Rows 2 and 3 are one fact rendered twice, once for a human and once for a machine. That is the thing to fix, and it is cheaper than a colour decision.

Candidates, none chosen:

1. **`stale_odds` goes muted.** The code is a *label*; the ochre sentence above it already carries the warning. Its own explanation line is already muted, so the code would sit with its explanation instead of with the warning. Cheapest, reversible, no new token.
2. **`stale_odds` becomes a bordered chip** rather than coloured text — weight instead of hue, which is the ADR 0061 §3 pattern and survives ADR 0081 untouched.
3. **Collapse rows 2 and 3 into one line.** Content fix, not a colour fix. Probably correct regardless of which colour wins, and it removes a whole line from 100 rows.
4. **Leave it.** Ochre-on-everything is honest when everything is refused, and the row's job per ADR 0071 is price transparency, not a hierarchy.

## What this ticket does NOT decide

- **Whether anything takes indigo.** That is #33, still unowned, and the zero-indigo observation above is evidence *for* #33 rather than a second ticket.
- **What the real-money warning strip wears.** #32.
- **Whether 100 rows should be on the screen.** #15 owns the cut.

## Evidence

- Live at `bc256e3`; ADR 0081 (`docs/adr/0081-the-brand-red-is-given-up-so-red-can-mean-lose.md`), §3 item 3 is the change that produced the third ochre line.
- The elements are `SlateRow.tsx:146` (the reason, moved by ADR 0081), `slate/page.tsx:491` and `:606` (the same reason on two other screens, moved with it), against `EDGE_TONE_CLASS.refused` in `api.ts:1407`, which was already ochre and is what the move was made consistent with.

children.title: The panel promised a sweep that the loop had already refused
children.body:
Part of #3

## The observation

Joe opened the desk at 2026-08-28 04:38Z. Every row said the books were **198 minutes old** and `Not actionable until the odds are refreshed`. Nothing was refreshing — and the refresh panel, on the same screen at the same moment, said:

> The next scheduled sweep is **now** and buys these same team lines out of the day's budget.

While the loop, at 04:38:25Z and again at 04:38:42Z, said:

> `no sweep: ... desk refresh cannot be served: the attention slice is 300 credits a day and 300 are spent; the hourly floor still runs`

**The page and the loop contradicted each other, simultaneously, on the one readout a human uses to decide whether to wait or act.**

## Why, and this is verified in the code rather than inferred

`next_sweep_ms` is `window_status().next_call_ms` (`timing.py:1072`), whose own comment states the design intent:

> *"Computed through `firing_for_slot`, the same predicate the loop fires on, **so the page cannot disagree with it**."*

That claim holds for the slot schedule and **fails for the budget**. The attention-slice check is not in `firing_for_slot`; it sits in the firing loop at **`timing.py:1701-1708`**, *after* the predicate has already said a call is wanted:

```python
on_the_floor = not attended and not desk_is_open(desk_window, now_ms)
if not on_the_floor and attention_spent + cost > attention_daily_credits:
    refused_for_cost.append(f"{sport_key} desk refresh cannot be served: ...")
    continue
```

So `next_call_ms` answers *"is a call wanted?"* and the screen renders it as *"is a call coming?"* — two different questions that agree on every night the slice has credits left, and diverge on the nights it does not. The docstring is right about the mechanism it names and wrong about the guarantee it claims.

**A tap would have worked.** 150 credits are reserved for taps and **0 had been used.** The one action that would have fixed the screen was sitting there unused, and the screen was actively telling the reader not to bother.

## The state that was actually true

Both automatic paths were correctly off (full working in #34):

- **attention slice spent** — 300 of 300, exhausted at 20:46:30Z the previous evening
- **hourly floor idle** — its rule is a fixture inside twelve hours; the next kickoff was ~13.7 h out

Nothing was broken. ADR 0071 §2.6 was doing exactly what it was built to do. The defect is that the desk was deliberately silent and told the reader the opposite.

## The question

**What does the refresh panel say when the automatic paths are off, and how does the reader tell "wait" from "tap"?**

Three states the panel currently renders identically:

| state | what is true | what the reader should do |
|---|---|---|
| **attended** | slice has credits, ~10 min cadence | wait, it is coming |
| **slice spent** | attention exhausted, floor may or may not apply | **tap** — 150 credits are sitting there |
| **nothing due** | no fixture inside twelve hours, floor correctly idle | tap, or accept stale prices for a game half a day away |

The middle row is where Joe was, and the only one where the tool withholds an action the reader would obviously want.

## Two things to settle, and the first is not a copy change

1. **Does `next_sweep_ms` become budget-aware, or does the panel stop rendering it as a promise?** Either fixes the contradiction; they are different products. Making the field budget-aware keeps one number honest everywhere it appears. Changing the sentence leaves the field lying to any future caller. The docstring's guarantee has to end up true or be deleted — a comment claiming the page cannot disagree, on a page that did, is worse than no comment.
2. **What the panel says in the other two states.** Copy, and it belongs with whoever owns the refresh panel's voice.

## Constraints, so this is not solved by shouting

- **Not an alarm.** Nothing is broken; ADR 0071 calls the slice *"a hard ceiling and the reason the design is safe."* A red banner would be a false alarm three nights in four. Colour is settled: a warning is `--accent-2` (ADR 0081), and this is a warning at most.
- **Must not manufacture action.** ADR 0071 §2.1 — the desk *"does not manufacture action and does not abstain on his behalf."* Telling him to tap because a number is stale, on a slate where `BETTABLE` is 0 and no row has ever cleared the fee, is manufacturing action. Reporting which state the system is in is not.
- **`sweeps_remaining_today` is computed from the whole day's budget** (`timing.py:1134`, `state.remaining_today // sweep_cost`), not from the attention slice. Anything built here should check whether that readout has the same defect before trusting it.

## Not in scope

- **Whether 300/day is the right ceiling.** A budget decision needing its own ticket. #34 measured what it buys — **4.88 hours of attention at 61 credits/hour** — and deliberately did not judge it.
- **Whether 100 unbettable rows belong on the screen.** #15.

## Evidence

- Screenshots of the live Games screen, 2026-08-28 04:38Z, live at `bc256e3`.
- `scripts/inspect_live_db.py sweep-log` and `credits-day --date 20260827`, read 04:4xZ.
- `backend/odds/timing.py:1021-1027` (the claim), `:1072` (the field), `:1701-1708` (the check that is not in it).

children.title: Props as parlay legs: measure NFL coverage, or kill the lane
children.body:
Part of #3

**Supersedes #12.** #12 is closed and correct on its own question; this is a different one, and closing it did not answer this.

## What changed

- **2026-09-02, #12:** *"option A — he does not really bet props; drop them from the brief."* The question there was props as **picks** — a prop on the slate, filtered, presented as something to bet.
- **2026-09-10:** *"i want to bet on props for parlay legs."* The question here is props as **legs** — a prop inside a parlay card, never surfaced as a pick of its own.

Both answers stand. A prop he would not bet alone is still a leg he would combine, so #12's answer does not decide this one, and this ticket does not overturn it. Neither should be edited to agree with the other.

## The mechanism, which is why this is not a UI ticket

The parlay leg pool is **odds-feed-driven**: the join runs `fair_prices` → find a Kalshi market, never the reverse (`backend/parlays.py`, `CANDIDATE_SQL` selects `FROM fair_prices`; the `kalshi_markets` lookup is keyed off event tickers that came out of it). A market Kalshi trades cannot become a parlay leg unless the odds feed bought a consensus price for it first.

So "add props as legs" is a **feed** decision wearing a UI request's clothes. It is one edit with two halves:

1. `PROP_SERIES = {**MLB_PROP_SERIES, **NFL_PROP_SERIES}` in `backend/kalshi/props.py`
2. a sport-aware `prop_market_keys()` in `backend/odds/client.py`

Half alone is broken both ways. And (2) is where the money is: `prop_market_keys()` returns a **flat list whose length is the price**, requested for every event of every sport — three NFL keys there would be bought on every MLB event too.

## What is already known

- **No new parser is needed.** The MLB grammar `"Player: N+"` and the join identity `floor_strike == N - 0.5` hold **2,029 of 2,029** across KXNFLPASSYDS (253), KXNFLRECYDS (1,160) and KXNFLRSHYDS (616) — three magnitudes, so it is a property of Kalshi's prop ladder rather than of baseball. Captured unauthenticated, zero credits (`8d5dd1c`).
- **KXNFLFIRSTTD joins to nothing**: 362 markets, **zero** `floor_strike`, bare-name subtitles, `strike_type = 'structured'`. No rung.
- **KXNFLANYTD is unmeasured, not tested** — 0 open events at capture time.
- `NFL_PROP_SERIES` is staged and tested; `PROP_SERIES` is unchanged, so live behaviour has not moved.

## What blocks it

1. **`backend/odds/` is under a change freeze until 10:00Z 2026-09-14.** Reading and citing it is fine; editing is not.
2. **Coverage is unmeasured and the prior is bad.** ADR 0079 put primary-only coverage at **48 of 263** MLB prop markets (18%), NFL ladders are longer, and **35,448 of 35,448** alternate rungs carry no Under and cannot be devigged. An unpriceable rung is not a leg.

## The decision this ticket needs from Joe

After the freeze lifts: **spend ~14 credits on one NFL event to measure prop coverage before building, or kill the lane on the MLB prior?**

If coverage is as bad as MLB's, the honest answer is that props cannot be legs often enough to be worth the per-sweep credit cost, and the lane closes with a number behind it instead of a guess.

## What this ticket does not ask

- It does not reopen props as **picks**. #12 answered that.
- It does not touch the `eu`-region / sharp-anchor trade, which ADR 0110 dates to 2026-09-28.

children.title: A prop refresh on a non-MLB fixture requests MLB markets and may still bill; refuse it
children.body:
Part of #3

**The defect.** `POST /api/odds/refresh` (`backend/api/routers/odds.py:125`) accepts any stored upcoming `odds_event_id` for the named `sport_key`, and the runner then buys props for it with `prop_market_keys()` (`backend/odds/client.py:140-185`), which returns the five MLB keys for every sport. A prop tap on an NFL or NCAAF fixture therefore requests `batter_hits` and friends against a football game. The Odds API answers with nothing useful and may still bill the call; the desk records a "served" refresh with no rows. The refreshable list (`GET /api/odds/refreshable`) advertises `prop_credits` for those fixtures as if the tap could buy something.

**Why it is live today.** The route is behind auth and reachable from the `StaleOddsExit` control on the desk. The only prop-capable sport is MLB, whose season ends in about two weeks, after which every prop tap on the desk is this defect.

**The fix the partner asked for: a refusal, not a build.** Reject a prop refresh (an `odds_event_id` tap) for any sport that has no prop keys, with the refusal reason rendered on the button the way the other `ondemand.submit` refusals are, and have `/api/odds/refreshable` report `prop_credits` as unavailable for those sports. Do not make `prop_market_keys()` sport-aware here; that is the NFL build #36 declined, and it belongs to a ticket opened as a build.

children.title: The Confirm button quotes a price that is not what leaves your account
children.body:
Part of #3. Opened 2026-09-16 under CLAUDE.md workflow step 7 (a question for Joe is a ticket, not a line). Answer with the ticket number and a letter; the recommendation is listed first.

## The question

The button you tap to spend real money reads `Confirm — buy 3 YES for $1.52`. That is contracts × ask. **Kalshi's fee is not in it.** You learn the fee-inclusive figure only on the receipt, after the order has gone. Should the fee be on the button?

**Terms.** The *ask* is the price you pay per contract. Kalshi charges a *fee* on top, largest near 50c (about 1.75c on a 50c contract at the coefficient the desk applies). *Break-even* is how often the bet has to win for you to come out at zero: at a 50c ask it is not 50%, it is ~51.75% once the fee is in. That 1.75 points is bigger than any edge this repo has ever measured; the whole headroom against a sportsbook is 0.63 points (CLAUDE.md, cost bars).

## Options

- **A (recommended):** the button carries the all-in figure and the line above it carries break-even — `Confirm — buy 3 YES for at most $1.63 (ask $1.52 + fee $0.11)` and *"you need this to happen more than 52.4% of the time to break even"*. Both computed on the server, nothing in TypeScript.
- **B:** all-in total on the button only, no break-even line.
- **C:** leave it. The receipt already says "at most".

## Evidence

- `frontend/src/components/ManualTicket.tsx:626-631` — the button is `dollars(contracts * facts.ask_tenths)`, fee excluded.
- `ManualTicket.tsx:576-579` and `:826` name the fee in prose ("plus the fee"; "the exact fee on this venue is still being measured") and never give the number.
- The number exists: `backend/kalshi/orders.py:307` `worst_case_cost_dollars`; `backend/api/routes.py:2984-3010` `_manual_worst_case_dollars` is combo-aware. It is called at `routes.py:3822`, **after** submission, and surfaces only in the Placed panel (`ManualTicket.tsx:953-958`).
- The preflight the ticket reads, `GET /api/manual/market/{ticker}` (`routes.py:3116-3117`), is "quote + book only — no fair value, no edge, no opinion (ADR 0062)". A fee is the venue's charge, not the tool's opinion, so the build needs a one-paragraph ADR 0062 amendment saying so, or the next session re-litigates it.
- The combo path already ships a server-worded fee note (`backend/parlays.py:320-324`); singles get nothing.

## What changes at the moment of a bet

The most-read number on the money path becomes the number you are actually charged. "Still being measured" is about the *true* fee; the *applied* fee is exact arithmetic (`TAKER_COEFFICIENT` 0.070; combos use a separate, higher coefficient with ceiling rounding, so "at most" holds on both).

Raised by the partner and sharp-bettor passes of 2026-09-16, independently, both first.

children.title: The ticket's ask has no age, and your limit is pinned to the price you opened it at
children.body:
Part of #3. Opened 2026-09-16 under CLAUDE.md workflow step 7 (a question for Joe is a ticket, not a line). Answer with the ticket number and a letter; the recommendation is listed first.

## The question

The ticket shows an ask with no clock on it, reads the price once when it opens, and pins your order's price limit to that opening ask. If the ask ticks up while you type, your immediate-or-cancel order is killed at the venue and the ticket says "refused" without saying why. What should the ticket do?

**Terms.** An *IOC* (immediate-or-cancel) order fills right now at your limit or dies; nothing rests on the book. *Quote age* is how long ago the desk last read the price. A price with no age is history, not a price.

## Options

- **A (recommended):** show the age beside each ask (`50.7c · read 8s ago`, ticking), and add a "re-read the book" button that re-fetches the price and re-pins the limit. **It informs and never blocks** — ADR 0112 removed five brakes and a staleness gate here would be a sixth under a new name.
- **B:** age only, no re-read. You learn the price is old and your only remedy is close-and-reopen.
- **C:** auto-refresh the ask every few seconds while the ticket is open. Refused by the sharp-bettor: a number that changes under your finger is how you tap the wrong price.
