children.title: Question for Joe: should the card stop saying the edge is completely real
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** an opportunity card tells you the edge is
"completely real" — should that sentence come off, given this repo measured
that edge and got a negative number?

## What the screen says

`frontend/src/components/OpportunityCard.tsx:202-224` renders, under the cost
block:

> $12.40 for the contracts and $0.31 in fees. All of it is lost if this settles
> the other way. The swing is **29**× the expected value, so 10 bets this shape
> end down **46%** of the time — **with the edge completely real.**

That last clause is the whole question.

**Terms, because they matter here:**

- **Expected value (EV)** — the average profit per bet *if the edge is real*.
- **Swing / standard deviation (SD)** — how much an individual bet bounces
  around that average. A big swing against a small EV means luck dominates.
- **Edge** — here, the gap between the sportsbook consensus price and Kalshi's
  price. It is the only thing the desk has ever had.

The sentence is saying: *even when you are genuinely right, variance alone
sinks you 46% of the time over ten bets.* That is true arithmetic. The problem
is the premise it grants for free.

## Why it contradicts our own record

`beta` is the number that asks whether that gap predicts anything. We measured
it twice:

    2026-08-16   beta = -0.141   interval [-0.334, +0.052]
    2026-08-25   beta = -0.076   interval [-0.173, +0.022]

Both intervals sit **entirely below** the 0.40 no-signal threshold, and both
arms are negative. CLAUDE.md's instruction for planning is "treat the signal as
settled negative."

The card's two inputs, `ev_net_dollars` and `sd_dollars`
(`backend/api/serialise.py:98-120`, `:502-510`), are both functions of
`fair_probability` — that same gap. So the sentence offers **variance as the
only reason you could lose**, on a quantity we measured and could not
distinguish from noise pointing the wrong way.

**This repo already refused exactly this composite once.**
`tests/test_trust_surfaces.py` excludes the edge term from the evidence score,
with the reason written in its docstring: *"a composite carrying the gap would
rank the least trustworthy rows highest."* Same gap, same file tree, opposite
conclusion.

## Where it actually shows, read off the served payloads today (2026-09-16)

- **On the live desk: nowhere, today.** `/api/board?include_suppressed=false`
  returns `surfaced: 0`, and the block is gated on `suggested_contracts > 0`.
  It is latent — it fires the moment a row gets sized again, which is exactly
  when you are about to bet.
- **On the public demo: right now.** `kalshi-cockpit-demo.fly.dev` serves
  `contracts=1, sd=0.498, ev=0.0174, losing_run_probability=0.456`, which
  renders the sentence above verbatim. That is the portfolio URL, and it is
  nine days / 206 commits stale (`69ba254`).

I checked one further claim and it is **false**, so it is not part of this
ticket: the bet slip does not print a `$0.00` swing. `liveSizing.ts` makes an
unsized row non-offerable, so that sheet cannot open on a zero-contract row.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Delete the sentence and both fields end-to-end.**
Remove the clause, the swing multiple, `losing_run_probability`,
`losing_run_bets` and `sd_dollars` from `serialise.py`, the card, the bet slip
and `api.ts`. Add a sweep test that enumerates the priced surfaces so it cannot
quietly come back, modelled on the one written yesterday
(`test_combo_exit_copy_is_small_and_unmeasured_on_every_surface.py`).
*On screen:* the cost block keeps "$12.40 for the contracts and $0.31 in fees.
All of it is lost if this settles the other way." — which is a fact about the
money, not a claim about the edge. You lose nothing you can act on.

**(B) Keep the swing figure, drop the EV clause.** Keep "Swing, 1 SD $0.50" as
a bare number; delete the sentence that divides it by EV and asserts the edge.
*On screen:* one dollar figure survives with no story attached. Honest, but it
still comes from the gap, so it is a precise number about something we
measured as noise.

**(C) Leave it.** *On screen:* nothing changes; the demo keeps saying it, and
the desk says it again the next time a row is sized.

My recommendation is **A**. The tool's job at the moment of a bet is price
transparency — what Kalshi charges against what the consensus says it is worth
(ADR 0071). "The edge is completely real" is not transparency; it is the one
claim our own measurements refuse to support.

*Evidence re-read on `main` = `5f4d1de` and off the live and demo served
payloads, 2026-09-16.*

children.title: Question for Joe: should the hedge value your stake at what Kalshi charged instead of what we sent
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** your ten open positions value what you staked
at the price we *sent* to Kalshi, not the price Kalshi actually charged you —
and since 2026-09-11 we have been storing the real number without reading it,
so should the hedge figure switch to it?

## The two prices

When you tap Confirm, two different numbers exist:

- **The sent price** — what we asked for. We write it to
  `manual_orders.limit_price_tenths` at *intent* time, before the venue has
  done anything (`backend/store/manual_orders.py:648`).
- **The fill price** — what you actually paid. Kalshi reports it back, and
  since schema v40 we store it on the same permanent row as
  `venue_avg_fill_price_tenths`, with `venue_fill_count` and
  `venue_avg_fee_dollars` beside it (`manual_orders.py:953`).

They are usually the same and sometimes not. The registered census on
2026-09-15 found them identical on **11 of 12** joined rows and apart by
**+22 tenths of a cent per contract** on the twelfth. That look is spent —
it cannot be re-run for a different answer.

## What is reading which

**Nothing that runs reads the venue's number.** I grepped the whole tree: the
only readers of `venue_avg_fill_price_tenths` are
`scripts/census_recorded_fill_vs_venue.py` (the spent census) and its tests.
No route, no screen, no live path.

Meanwhile `backend/api/routes.py:4576` writes

    stake_tenths = contracts * fill_price_tenths

off the **sent** price, under a comment that reads *"Stake is what he paid."*
That comment is false. `backend/hedge.py:769` then computes the hedge figure
from `position["stake_tenths"]`, across all **10 open positions**.

So: we measured the error, banked the fix in the schema, and left the money
path pointed at the old number. ADR 0143 §4 deferred the rewire eleven days ago
as *"a money-path change with its own decision to make"* — and nobody has made
the decision.

## Why this is your call and not a cleanup

It touches the money path, it needs a new ADR and probably a schema version,
and it changes a number on a screen you use during a live game. It also has a
genuine design fork — see (B).

**Terms:** a **hedge** is a second bet on the other side that locks in part of
a result while a game is still running. Its figure depends on what you already
sank, which is the stake. **Tenths** are tenths of a cent, the integer unit
this repo uses for all money.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Rewire the stake to the venue's number, fall back to the
sent price.** Where `venue_avg_fill_price_tenths` exists on the row, use it;
where it is NULL (pre-v40 rows, and the one unfilled order) keep the sent price
and say so. New ADR, likely schema v45, and a test pinning both branches.
*On screen:* the hedge figure moves by up to a couple of cents a contract on
positions where the fill differed, and stops silently claiming a price you may
not have paid.

**(B) Rewire the stake *and* the entry fee.** Same as A, plus use the venue's
own `venue_avg_fee_dollars` instead of our computed fee. Bigger: it removes
error term E3 rather than shrinking it, but the venue's fee is a dollar float
and this repo keeps money in integer tenths, so it needs a conversion rule
decided in advance.
*On screen:* same as A, slightly more accurate, more code.

**(C) Leave it, and fix the lie instead.** Change the comment at
`routes.py:4571-4576` to say the stake is the sent price, and add a line to the
hedge screen saying the figure is based on what was asked, not what was
charged.
*On screen:* the figure does not move; one more caveat appears on `/hedge`.

I recommend **A**. The correct number is already on the row — we are choosing
not to read it. (C) is the honest version of doing nothing, and it is a real
option if you would rather not touch the money path while the season is live;
say so and I will take C today and leave A for a quiet week.

*Evidence re-read on `main` = `5f4d1de`, 2026-09-16.*

children.title: Question for Joe: the receipt calls the sent price a fill - rename it or show the real one
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** the glossary defines "fill" as *"what you
truly paid"*, and the figure it pops open from is the price we sent, not the
price you paid — should the label change, the definition change, or both?

## The exact contradiction

Tap the **Fill** figure on the order receipt and the popover says
(`frontend/src/lib/glossary.ts:267-272`):

> **fill** — An order actually matching: the moment your buy found a seller.
> The fill price is what you truly paid, and it can differ from the ask you
> were looking at.

The figure it is attached to (`TicketSheet.tsx:787-791`) is
`order.fill_price_display`, which the server fills in at
`backend/api/routes.py:2848`:

    "fill_price_display": format_price(order.fill_price_tenths)

`order` there is an `OrderRequest` — the thing we are about to send.
`OrderRequest.fill_price_tenths` is defined at
`backend/kalshi/orders.py:299` as *"what one contract of our side costs at the
price being sent."* `OrderOutcome` — the venue's reply — has no such property
at all.

So the popover teaches you that this number is the one that can differ from the
ask, when it is in fact derived from the ask. The sentence is wrong in the
direction that sounds reassuring: it claims the screen is showing you reality
when it is showing you intent.

This is narrower than the stake-basis question in the sibling ticket — that one
is about the hedge arithmetic on ten open positions, this one is about a word
on a receipt. I kept it separate because the fix is small enough to ship on its
own today.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Rename the figure, leave the glossary alone.**
Label it **"Limit"** or **"Sent price"** instead of "Fill", and drop the
`<Term k="fill">` wrapper from it. The glossary's definition of *fill* stays
exactly as written, because it is correct — it just was not describing this
number.
*On screen:* one word changes on the order receipt. Nothing else moves, no
server change, no test rewrite beyond the label.

**(B) Keep the label, weaken the definition.** Change the glossary to say the
fill price is "what we asked to pay". *On screen:* the popover text changes.
I do not recommend it: it makes the glossary wrong about the industry term so
that one screen can stay wrong about its own number, and "fill" has a real
meaning you will meet everywhere else.

**(C) Show the real fill.** Since schema v40 the venue's own average fill price
is on the row (`venue_avg_fill_price_tenths`). Render that where it exists.
*On screen:* the receipt gains a genuinely correct Fill figure. This is the
best answer but it is the sibling ticket's work — if you pick A here and A
there, we can do C as a follow-on for free.

Recommendation **A**, because it is true immediately and costs one word.

*Evidence re-read on `main` = `5f4d1de`, 2026-09-16.*

children.title: Question for Joe: delete the ANALYZE park, or rewrite it to name the cold path it was really about
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** we parked a piece of database-tuning work
behind a trigger that turns out to have already fired twice — should the park be
deleted, or rewritten to name the real condition?

## Background, in plain terms

SQLite picks how to run each query. It picks better when it has **table
statistics** — a small summary of how big each table is and how varied each
column is. Running `ANALYZE` builds them.

On 2026-09-16 we found the live database has **no table statistics at all** and
never has. Every query plan on the box has been chosen from built-in guesses
since first boot. That finding is banked in ADR 0159 and needs nothing further.

Whether to actually *run* `ANALYZE` was left undecided, and parked behind this
trigger (`tasks/NEXT.md:341`):

> unpark only if a route-latency read shows a desk route over the 25 s read
> budget **and** the plan implicates `fair_prices`.

The **read budget** is a 25-second ceiling on any single API read; past it the
request is killed and the screen says "Backend unreachable" (ADR 0135).

## What I found today

I ran the route-latency read. On a warm box every desk route came back between
75 ms and 1.7 s — nowhere near 25 s. My first draft concluded the trigger was
false and deleted the park.

**That was wrong, and an audit caught it.** I measured the one condition where
the budget was known in advance not to fire. The budget has actually been
reached **twice**:

    2026-09-15  /api/slate?league=americanfootball_nfl   6 incidents in 5 min
                cause: a missing index path in the league filter
                FIXED same day (commit 2d8de82, 13:57Z), deployed, test-pinned

    2026-09-10  /api/parlays                             503 read_budget_exceeded
                cause: two full-table reads evicted the page cache;
                the parlay query then took 74.8 s cold -- 3x the budget
                NOT FIXED. Structural.

The second one is why this is a question. The box has 2 GB of RAM and no swap,
the database is 5.43 GB, and the page cache tops out near 1.49 GB — so **at
most ~27% of the file can ever be in memory**. `warm_read_path.py` puts it
bluntly: "every restart is a coin flip on a 503, and restarts are not rare."

So the trigger as written has been satisfied. It just was not satisfied by the
thing it was watching for.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Retire the ANALYZE line on a different, stronger
argument, and delete the park.**
Not on my warm timings. On this line from ADR 0159's own rehearsal:

    CANDIDATE_SQL   1,177 ms -> 1,157 ms   1.02x   plan UNCHANGED

`CANDIDATE_SQL` is the query behind `/api/parlays` — the desk's slowest route
and the one with the real 503. `ANALYZE` changed it by 2% and did not change
its plan at all. A "no change" result like that does not depend on the timing
defect that makes the rehearsal's other numbers unreliable, and it holds on a
cold box, a big Saturday slate and a cache eviction alike.
*What changes:* one queue item goes away. Nothing on the desk was waiting for
it. If anyone wants `ANALYZE` later they open it fresh on its own merits rather
than inheriting a stale trigger.

**(B) Rewrite the park to name the real condition.** Keep a park, but point it
at the thing that actually bites: the cold and cache-evicted path, not a warm
route timing. Something like "revisit if a 503 at the read budget recurs on a
route whose plan reads `fair_prices`, on a box that has not been restarted."
*What changes:* the queue item stays, but it now describes a condition that can
genuinely be observed. Costs nothing until it fires.

**(C) Leave the park exactly as written.** *What changes:* nothing — but the
trigger stays ambiguous, and the next session to run a latency read will reach
the same wrong conclusion I did.

I recommend **A**, with one caveat I want on the record: A retires the
*tuning* work, it does not address the 27% residency ceiling. That is a
separate and bigger question about the box, and nothing here should be read as
saying the cold-start 503 is solved. It is not.

*Evidence: `docs/measurements/2026-09-16-desk-route-latency-warm-box.md`
(rewritten after audit), ADR 0159, and the 2026-09-10 incident recorded in
session memory.*

children.title: Question for Joe: how should the Board teach a losing week now that the edge clause is gone
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** the Board's "How to read this" panel has a
bullet teaching you how to survive a losing week, and after today's trim its
remaining premise still assumes the edge is there — should it be re-worded,
and to what?

## What happened

You answered `48A` and the "with the edge completely real" clause came off the
opportunity card. A lane found the **same claim in prose**, in a place the
brief never named: `frontend/src/components/HowToRead.tsx`, the Board's
teaching panel. Before today it read:

> **The swing is far larger than the edge, every time.** A bet worth
> twenty-six cents in expectation still moves seven or eight dollars either way
> when it settles. Ten bets like that end the week down almost half the time
> *with the edge completely real*, so a losing week is not evidence the tool is
> broken and is not a reason to bet bigger.

The clause and the run sentence were trimmed under 48A. It now reads:

> **The swing is far larger than the edge, every time.** A bet worth
> twenty-six cents in expectation still moves seven or eight dollars either way
> when it settles, so a losing week is not evidence the tool is broken and is
> not a reason to bet bigger.

## Why that is still a question

The trim removed the explicit claim. The **premise underneath it survives**:
"the swing is far larger than *the edge*" and "a losing week is not evidence
the tool is broken" both presuppose there is an edge that a losing week is
failing to reveal.

On the measured record there is no edge to be larger than. `beta = -0.141` and
`-0.076`, both intervals entirely below the 0.40 no-signal threshold, both
arms negative.

**But the advice is still good advice**, which is exactly why this is yours
and not a lane's. "A losing week is not a reason to bet bigger" is true
regardless of whether any edge exists — it is the single most useful sentence
on that panel, and deleting it to be technically pure would make the screen
worse. This is teaching copy, and how to teach variance honestly without
implying a payoff is a judgement call about what you want to be told.

**Term:** *variance* is the ordinary bounce in results that has nothing to do
with whether a bet was good. It is the reason a good bettor can lose for weeks
and a bad one can win for weeks.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Re-word to teach variance without an edge.**
Something like: *"The swing is far larger than any edge on this screen. A bet
worth twenty-six cents in expectation still moves seven or eight dollars either
way when it settles — so a week's results tell you almost nothing, and a losing
week is not a reason to bet bigger."*
*On screen:* same bullet, same length, same lesson. It stops implying the edge
is real and keeps the part that protects you.

**(B) Keep it as trimmed today.** *On screen:* nothing further changes. The
explicit claim is gone; the presupposition stays. Defensible if you read the
bullet as being about bet sizing rather than about the edge.

**(C) Cut the bullet.** *On screen:* four bullets instead of five, and the one
sentence that tells you not to chase losses is gone. I do not recommend this.

I recommend **A**. You asked to be educated rather than shielded, and the
honest version of this lesson is stronger than the current one: *a week tells
you nothing* is a better thing to know than *a week tells you nothing when the
edge is real*.

*Found while building #48A; the trim is already on `main`. Nothing further
ships on this bullet until you answer.*

children.title: Question for Joe: should the hedge card say which stake basis a ticket is on
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** after today's fix, some of your ten open
positions compute the hedge off the price Kalshi actually charged and some off
the price we sent, and the card does not say which — should it?

## What changed today

You answered `49A`. The hedge figure now reads the venue's own fill price
where it can, and falls back to the sent price where it cannot. That shipped
as ADR 0160.

The fallback is not rare, and it is not a bug. A position falls back when any
of these is true:

- **It is a sportsbook slip, not a Kalshi combo.** No order row exists; the
  stake is the figure you typed and always was.
- **The bet predates 11 September**, when we started storing the venue's
  number. Seven of your thirteen real orders are older than that.
- **The order was a NO.** Deliberately refused — our stored price reflects a
  NO onto the YES book and the venue's does not, and which book Kalshi quoted
  on a NO has never been established. Reading it anyway could halve or double
  the stake. All thirteen of your real orders are YES, so this has not come up
  yet, but the path exists.
- The link between the position and the order is unreadable, or the contract
  counts disagree.

So on any given day some of your open tickets are on Kalshi's number and some
are on ours. The underlying `stake_basis` is served on `/api/hedge` for an
auditor — **it is not on the card.**

## Why this is a question and not just a build

Adding a label is easy. Whether it helps you mid-game is the part I cannot
decide.

The argument for: the whole point of #49 was that a figure should not quietly
claim a price you may not have paid. A card that is sometimes on one basis and
sometimes on the other, saying neither, has the same shape of problem one
level up.

The argument against: you look at `/hedge` while a game is running and a leg
is in danger. That is the worst possible moment to add a word you have to
think about. The difference between the two bases was **zero on 11 of 12
measured rows**, and 22 tenths of a cent per contract on the twelfth — small
against a figure already carrying four error terms.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Say it only when it is the fallback, in small type.**
A venue-priced ticket says nothing extra. A fallback ticket carries a short
line — e.g. *"stake as recorded — bet predates the venue's fill record"* —
naming the actual reason from the eight we already compute.
*On screen:* most tickets look exactly as they do now. The older ones gain one
grey line. Nothing is added to the moment you are reading the number.

**(B) Label both.** Every ticket says which basis it is on.
*On screen:* a consistent line on every card. Honest and symmetric, but it
spends attention on a distinction that is zero for most positions — and it is
the same "states the freshness fact four times" problem the sharp-bettor
flagged on the Games row.

**(C) Say nothing; leave it for the auditor.** The field stays on `/api/hedge`
for anyone reading the payload, and the card stays as it is.
*On screen:* nothing changes. Defensible — the measured difference is small
and the card is already dense.

I recommend **A**. It follows the rule we have been applying all day — a
warning that fires only on the good case reads as a check that passed, so the
line should appear on the case that is *less* certain, not the more certain
one.

*Raised by the lane that built #49A; it could not open this itself. ADR 0160 §5
records the field being served and deliberately not declared to the frontend.*

children.title: Question for Joe: what should the sharp-anchor base rate show on Picks, where every row is a moneyline
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** you approved showing the sharp-book base rate
per (league, market family) on the Games slate — but on Picks that grouping
collapses to just "per league", so what should Picks show?

## What you already decided

On 2026-09-16 you chose **option A**: show the base rate up top, counting how
many rows on the screen had a sharp book behind them. It shipped in `432cbb9`
as `AnchorBaseRate`, grouped **per (league, market family)** — deliberately,
because NCAAF `h2h` anchors ~84% while NCAAF `spreads` anchors ~30%, and
pooling those describes neither.

A later session filed "put it on Picks too" as a build that was *decided in
principle*. **It is not**, and that is what I need you to settle.

## Why Picks is a different population

Two facts, both read on `main`:

- `anchored_on_sharp` already reaches the Picks payload (`routes.py:1646`).
  `consensus_market` does **not** — the ranking loop drops it.
- **Picks ranks one row per game, and that row is always the moneyline
  favourite.** So on Picks, `consensus_market` is constant: every row is `h2h`.

Which means the grouping you approved — per (league, market family) — would
have exactly one market family per league on that screen. It degenerates into
"per league", which is the pooling you were shown evidence against.

**Terms:** a *market family* is the kind of bet — moneyline (`h2h`, who wins),
spread (margin), total (combined score). A *sharp book* is one of the few
bookmakers whose prices are informative enough that we anchor our fair-value
estimate on them; when none is available we fall back to softer books and the
row says so.

So the question isn't "should Picks have the block" — it's "what does the block
mean on a screen where the distinction it exists to draw doesn't exist".

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Put it on Picks, grouped by league, and say `moneyline`
out loud.** One line per league: *"Pro Baseball — 7 of 11 moneyline picks had
a sharp book behind them."* Naming the market family in the sentence is what
stops it reading as a claim about the league's spreads and totals, which it is
not.
*On screen:* one or two short lines above the Picks list. Same counts-never-a-
percentage rule, same "every group listed including the fully-anchored ones",
same silence on `null`.

**(B) Leave Picks alone.** The per-row marker is already there on every Picks
row; only the denominator is missing.
*On screen:* nothing changes. Defensible — Picks is a short list you can eyeball,
and the block earns its place on Games because that screen is long.

**(C) Put it on Picks with no market-family wording.** Just "Pro Baseball — 7 of
11". *On screen:* shortest version. I do not recommend it: an unqualified
fraction on a moneyline-only screen reads as a statement about the league, and
that is precisely the pooling the Games version was built to avoid.

I recommend **A**. The block's whole value is that its denominator is honest;
on Picks the denominator is honest only if the sentence says what it counted.

*Raised because a previous session filed this as already-decided and it was
not — you answered about the Games slate, and Picks is a different population.*

children.title: Question for Joe: the positions screen has 503'd on a box too small for the database - pay for a bigger one?
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** the positions screen has returned "Backend
unreachable" in production, the cause is that the box is too small for the
database, and fixing it properly costs money — so do we pay, or work around it?

## What happened, twice

There is a 25-second ceiling on any single read. Past it the request is killed
and the screen says the backend is unreachable (ADR 0135). It has been hit
twice:

    15 Sep   the NFL chip on Games      6 times in 5 minutes
             a missing index path -- FIXED that day, deployed, test-pinned

    10 Sep   /api/parlays               503, read budget exceeded
             the parlay query then took 74.8 s -- three times the ceiling
             NOT FIXED

**The second one is the problem, and `/api/parlays` is the positions screen** —
what you open while a game is running to see what you hold.

## Why it is structural and not a bug

The box has **2 GB of RAM and no swap**. The database is **5.43 GB**. The
operating system's disk cache tops out near 1.49 GB, so **at most about 27% of
the database can ever be in memory at once.**

When the needed pages are in memory the query takes ~2 seconds. When they are
not, it reads them off disk and takes 75. Nothing is broken; the machine is
just too small to hold the working set.

Two consequences, from the code's own notes:

- **Every restart is a coin flip on a 503**, and restarts are not rare — every
  deploy is one.
- **Any large read elsewhere evicts the cache.** On 10 Sep a background
  analysis read a big table, and your next tap paid for it minutes later,
  which is why nobody connected the two at the time.

**Term:** the *page cache* is the operating system keeping recently-read parts
of a file in memory so the next read is fast. It is not something we configure;
it is whatever RAM is left over.

## Why this is your call

One branch costs money every month and the other costs engineering time that
might not work. I do not think I should pick that for you.

I also want to be straight about a limit: **I have not measured the cold path.**
Tonight's timings were all on a warm box and showed 75 ms to 1.7 s. That says
nothing about the case that actually fails, and a measurement that looks
reassuring about the wrong condition is how I got this wrong once already
today.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Pay for a bigger machine.**
Fly's next size up is 4 GB. That roughly doubles what can stay cached; 8 GB
would hold most of the working set. Rough order of magnitude: single-digit to
low-double-digit dollars a month more than now.
*What changes:* the 503 becomes rare or stops. No code risk, no new failure
mode, reversible in one command if it does not help.
*What it does not do:* it does not make the database smaller, so the same
problem returns as the record grows.

**(B) Make the query need less.** Bound or cache the parlay read so it touches
fewer pages.
*What changes:* possibly nothing. If the cost is genuinely "the pages are not
resident," a narrower query may still miss cache and still take 75 s — we would
spend the work to find that out. There is precedent for the work paying off
(bounding one census this week was worth 322×), but that query was reading rows
it did not need; this one may not be.

**(C) Prune the database.** Old rows we no longer read.
*What changes:* a smaller file fits a bigger fraction in cache. But it is a
one-way deletion of the record this project exists to keep, and it needs its
own decision about what is safe to lose.

**(D) Leave it.** It has happened once in production.
*What changes:* nothing. Accept an occasional "Backend unreachable" on the
positions screen, including right after any deploy.

I recommend **A**, and I would pair it with measuring the cold path properly
afterwards so we know whether it worked rather than assuming. If the monthly
cost matters more than the occasional 503, **D is a legitimate answer** and I
would not argue hard against it — it has fired once.

*Evidence: `docs/measurements/2026-09-16-desk-route-latency-warm-box.md` §D and
the residency figures in `scripts/warm_read_path.py`.*

children.title: Question for Joe: what should a hand-recorded position say instead of 'no Kalshi order matches this ticket'
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** five of your seventeen open positions now
carry a line saying "No Kalshi order matches this ticket" — which is true but
misleading, because those are parlays you recorded by hand and there never was
a ticket to match.

## Where this came from

You answered `53A` tonight: an `as_recorded` hedge ticket names the specific
reason its stake is not Kalshi's own number. That shipped and is live.

Verifying the deploy I read all seventeen positions. The split:

    ids 1-4      as_recorded, no_venue_price   bets before 11 Sep -- correct
    ids 5-10     venue_fill                    placed through the tool
    ids 11-15    as_recorded, no_order_row     <-- these five
    ids 16-17    venue_fill                    placed tonight, 00:36Z

Positions 11–15 have **no ticker and no timestamp at all** — both empty. Their
labels are yours: "Three totals", "Safe", "Next 3 hours".

I checked whether that was a bug and it is not. The code that records a
position has two callers: the order path, which fills in the ticker, and the
hand-record path on `/hedge`, where you type a ticket in and there is no Kalshi
order behind it in our records. **A hand-recorded parlay with no ticker is a
designed state**, and the desk is right to refuse to claim a price it cannot
source.

## The problem is only the sentence

It currently reads:

> No Kalshi order matches this ticket, so the stake above is the price recorded
> with it, not Kalshi's own record of the fill.

That implies we searched for a ticket and came up empty — as if something might
be missing. Nothing is missing. There is a sentence already written for this
exact situation, used when the position is a sportsbook slip:

> There was never a Kalshi order behind it, so the stake above is the figure
> you typed in.

It does not fire here, because these positions are tagged as Kalshi combos —
which they are. You placed them on Kalshi; you just recorded them by hand
instead of buying through the ticket screen.

**29% of your open positions read the slightly-wrong sentence.**

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Add a reason for "recorded by hand" and say that.**
Something like: *"You recorded this one by hand, so the stake above is the
figure you typed in — not Kalshi's record of what it charged."* The existing
`no_order_row` sentence stays for the case it was written for: a position that
DOES have a ticker but still finds no order, which would be a real bookkeeping
failure and should keep reading like one.
*On screen:* those five lines change wording. Nothing else moves. It also means
a genuine gap would stand out instead of hiding among five false alarms.

**(B) Leave the wording.** It is not false — no order does match.
*On screen:* nothing changes. Fair if you read the line as a statement about
our records rather than about your bet.

**(C) Say nothing on a hand-recorded position.** Treat "you typed this in" as
self-evident and render no line.
*On screen:* five lines disappear. I do not recommend it: the line's job is to
say why the stake is not Kalshi's number, and that reason is just as real when
you typed it.

I recommend **A**. The distinction it buys is worth more than the wording: once
"hand-recorded" has its own reason, a position that has a ticker and *still*
cannot find its order becomes visible instead of being lost in the same bucket.

*This is a build either way — you already settled the principle in `53A`. I am
asking because the sentence is yours, not because the fix is unclear.*

children.title: Question for Joe: is the props 'Price on Kalshi' tap still wanted, or should it be retired
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** the props card's "Price on Kalshi" button has
sat on the open list for weeks marked "JOE ONLY — a session must not do it", and
nobody has ever pressed it, so is it still wanted?

## Why it is on the list at all

Pressing it asks Kalshi to price a combination that does not exist yet. If no
market matches your legs, **Kalshi mints one on the exchange** — a real, public
market with your combination in it. That is an outward-facing act on a live
venue, so a session must not trigger it on your behalf, and none has.

The path is built and has been for weeks (ADR 0070, Slice C). It is not
blocked, broken or waiting on anything. It is waiting on you.

## Why I am asking rather than leaving it

It has been carried on the open list through at least three sessions unchanged.
An item that no one can execute and no one has decided on is the exact thing
that decays — it survives every rewrite because it is easy to copy forward, and
nobody ever asks whether it is still wanted.

Two facts worth having before you answer:

- **The build already tells you it often fails.** `backend/parlays.py:312`
  composes the message *"Pressing 'Price on Kalshi' often comes back with no
  price."* So a tap is not guaranteed to produce anything useful.
- **Your props answer has moved once already.** In September you said you do
  not really bet props as picks (#12), then later asked for props as parlay
  *legs* (#36) — not a reversal, a different question. This button is about
  props-as-legs, the live one.

**Term:** *minting* a market means the exchange creates it because someone asked
for a price on a combination nobody had listed yet. It becomes tradeable by
anyone, not just you.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. You press it once, when you next have a props parlay you
would actually bet.** No work from me. Tell me what came back and I will read
the row.
*What changes:* we learn whether the path works end-to-end against the real
venue, which no test can tell us. Costs one tap, at a moment you were going to
bet anyway — so it does not manufacture action.

**(B) I build something that makes the tap more informative first** — e.g. show
what will be sent and which collection it will try before you commit.
*What changes:* a screen gains a preview. But we would be improving a path whose
basic viability is still unconfirmed, which is the wrong order.

**(C) Retire it.** The lookup path stays in the code (it is used elsewhere) but
the item comes off the open list and stops being carried.
*What changes:* nothing on screen. One less thing on a list. Honest if you do
not see yourself pressing it — and if that is the answer, say so plainly and I
will record it as decided rather than pending.

I recommend **A**, with no deadline attached. If it has not happened in another
month, **C is the right answer and I would rather record that than carry it a
fourth time.**

children.title: Question for Joe: the 4 GB box buys weeks, and odds_snapshots has no retention rule - what is the plan?
children.body:
**The question in one sentence:** you just paid for a 4 GB box on my
recommendation, and the growth arithmetic says it buys weeks rather than a
fix — so what is the plan for the one table that has no retention rule at all?

## First, a correction you are owed

When I put #55 in front of you I showed a "free option E" that would shrink the
database to ~2.9 GB. **That was wrong twice**, and you answered with it on the
screen:

1. **The dedup already shipped**, on 2026-09-09, as ADR 0133 (`e8ec6ff`). I
   presented a deployed change as an unregistered opportunity.
2. **A dedup does not shrink the database.** Its own source document says so in
   a section titled *"It does not establish that a dedupe reclaims a single
   existing byte"*: it deletes nothing, touches no row already written, and
   *"changes the slope, not the level."*

Your answer still stands in substance — the box purchase was decided on the
residency arithmetic alone and is unaffected, and the second half became
"check whether the thing we already shipped is working", which is registered
for tomorrow. But you chose against an option I described wrongly.

## The arithmetic that makes this a question

    growth if the shipped dedup does nothing     326.6 MB/day   ~5.9 days to 50% residency
    growth if it works perfectly                 141.0 MB/day  ~13.7 days
    what a 30-day billing month would need      <=64.3 MB/day   unreachable

**No achievable dedup result buys one billing month of >=50% residency on a
4 GB box**, because the growth that is *not* `fair_prices` is on its own
141.0 MB/day against a 64.3 MB/day requirement.

That does not make the purchase wrong. The 503 is real, it has fired in
production, and $5-10/month is cheap against it. But 4 GB is a **stopgap
measured in weeks**, and you should hear that from me now rather than from the
positions screen failing again in a month.

**Term:** *residency* is the share of the database the machine can hold in
memory at once. Above roughly 50% the slow query stays fast; below it, a read
that misses memory goes to disk and can blow the 25-second ceiling that turns
into "Backend unreachable".

## The thing nobody owns

`odds_snapshots` is the residual growth term at roughly **141 MB/day, and it
has no retention rule.** Verified: `kalshi_quotes` is pruned, `fair_prices` is
pruned, and there is no `DELETE` against `odds_snapshots` anywhere in the
codebase. It grows forever by default, not by decision.

Every other big table got a retention decision at some point. This one never
did.

## The options

**(A) — RECOMMENDED. Let tomorrow's measurement report first, then decide.**
The registered read (2026-09-18, 07:00-11:00Z) tells us whether the shipped
dedup is working, which picks between the 5.9-day and 13.7-day columns. It is
two bounded queries and costs nothing.
*What changes:* nothing yet. You get a real number instead of a range, and the
retention question arrives with evidence attached. The risk is small: a month
of drift, against a failure that has fired once.

**(B) Decide the retention rule now, without waiting.** Pick how long raw
sportsbook snapshots are worth keeping — 30 days, 90, a season — and I build
the prune.
*What changes:* growth drops immediately and permanently. But it is a one-way
deletion of the record this project exists to keep, and "how long is this worth
keeping" is exactly the kind of question that deserves the evidence in (A).

**(C) Plan to keep buying RAM.** Treat the bill as the cost of keeping
everything, and raise it again when the 503 returns.
*What changes:* nothing now; roughly +$5-10/month each time, and the interval
between upgrades shortens as the file grows. Honest if the record matters more
than the bill — but worth saying out loud rather than arriving at by default,
which is what happens if nobody answers this.

**(D) Accept the 503s and stop paying to avoid them.** Revert to 2 GB.
*What changes:* saves the money; the positions screen breaks occasionally,
including after every deploy.

I recommend **A**, and I want to be clear it is the *cheap* answer rather than
the *right* one — it defers a decision by one day to buy a real number. If you
would rather just settle the retention rule now, **B is defensible** and I will
put the specific windows in front of you.

*Raised because I recommended a purchase on partly wrong reasoning and the
correction changes what happens next. Evidence:
`docs/measurements/2026-09-17-preregistration-fair-prices-dedup.md`, ADR 0163,
and #55 Amendment 2.*

children.title: Question for Joe: taking a maker's quote bets up to 90% of the combinations shard and the button never shows the dollars - what size should the desk ask for?
children.body:
**Question:** when you take a maker's quote on a combination, what size should the desk ask for?

Today the desk decides for you, and the button never shows the dollars.

**Terms.** *RFQ* (request for quote): you ask Kalshi's makers to price a combination privately; they answer; you take one answer or none. *Maker*: the person quoting you a price. A quote is all-or-nothing at the size you asked for. *Shard*: Kalshi keeps combination collateral in its own pool, separate from singles.

**Options**

- **(A) Recommended: you type a dollar amount each time, on the Ask-the-market form, with a remembered last value.** Same discipline as the singles ticket, where you type contracts and read dollars. The button then says "Take it: $4.80 all-in for 8.1 contracts at 59.3c".
- **(B) A default you set once** (e.g. $5) in settings, editable per ask.
- **(C) Keep today's behaviour: as much as the shard allows**, but print the dollar figure on the button so you see it before tapping.

**Evidence**

- `frontend/src/components/PriceOnKalshi.tsx:283` mounts `<AskTheMarket targetCostDollars="5.0000">`, hardcoded.
- `backend/combo_rfq.py:85,195`: `SHARD_HEADROOM = 0.90`; the ask is trimmed to 90% of the combinations shard's available balance. So the size is min($5.00, 90% of the shard). On the 2026-09-17 balance (#61, $5.79) that is about $5.20, most of the shard.
- `frontend/src/components/AskTheMarket.tsx`: the Take-it button shows the per-contract price and a contract count; no dollar figure anywhere.

**What changes on screen.** (A): one input on the ask form, dollars on the button. (B): a setting plus dollars on the button. (C): dollars on the button only.

**Not a brake.** ADR 0112 removed the five ceilings on your word and they stay gone. Choosing your own stake is not a ceiling; the venue's pool choosing it for you is a default nobody picked.

children.title: Question for Joe: may the hedge screen ask the makers what they would pay for a combination you hold, and should selling be armed there?
children.body:
**Question:** may the hedge screen fire a sell-side RFQ on a combination you hold, to show what a maker would pay you for it right now? And if yes, should selling be armed from that screen, or should it show the price and leave the sale to the Kalshi app?

**Terms.** *Sell-side RFQ*: asking the makers what they would pay to take your combination off you (the exit price), as opposed to what they would charge to sell you one. *Cost basis*: what you paid per contract. *Resting bid*: an order already sitting on the public book to buy at a stated price.

**Options**

- **(A) Recommended: show both exit prices, read-only, no selling from the desk.** On each open position: the best resting public-book bid, and the best bid a sell-side RFQ draws, beside your cost basis. Asking commits nothing (you already authorised asking in #59). Selling stays in the Kalshi app.
- **(B) Show the public-book bid only** (a free Kalshi read, no RFQ). Misses the exit on positions whose book is empty, which was 1 of your 3 on 2026-09-17.
- **(C) Show both and arm a Sell button**, same shape as Take-it. Spends nothing but ends a position on one tap.

**Evidence**

- 2026-09-17: sell-side RFQs on all three positions you hold drew a YES bid on 3 of 3, 16 of 44 quotes, every one at full size; two of the three also had resting public-book bids 38,709 and 24,900 contracts deep (`docs/measurements/2026-09-17-combinations-can-be-exited.md`).
- Neither surface dominated: the book beat the RFQ on two (5.10c vs 4.70c; 0.32c vs 0.14c), the RFQ was the only exit on the third.
- Every best bid sat below your cost (7.60 vs 10.20, 4.70 vs 5.70, 0.14 vs 0.38). An exit existing is not an exit being good, which is exactly why the price belongs on the screen and a recommendation does not.
- `/hedge` today shows only what hedging the endangered leg would cost (ADR 0078); it shows no exit price.

**What changes on screen.** (A)/(C): two prices per open combination next to cost basis; (C) adds a button that spends. (B): one price.

children.title: Question for Joe: the Parlays lede still says hardly anyone is bidding to buy a combination back - what should it say?
children.body:
**Question:** your Parlays page lede still ends "once you own one hardly anyone is bidding to buy it back". All three of your combinations drew a bid on 2026-09-17. What should that clause say?

This is your ratified copy (re-ratified 2026-09-10), so it is asked, not rewritten. It is the fourth false-availability sentence; #60 fixed the other three (checkbox, fallback note, card) with your answer (a): say what an exit *costs*, not how often it exists.

**Options**

- **(A) Recommended: same rule as #60, on the lede.** "…a card pays only if every pick on it wins, and selling one back before the outcome usually costs more than holding it." States the cost, asserts no frequency.
- **(B) Drop the clause.** "…a card pays only if every pick on it wins." Says nothing about exits; the checkbox already does.
- **(C) Keep it.** Only if you read "hardly anyone" as still true; the record says otherwise.

**Evidence**

- `frontend/src/app/parlays/page.tsx:136-141`, live on the demo.
- `docs/measurements/2026-09-17-combinations-can-be-exited.md`: 3 of 3 held combinations drew sell-side bids; two carry resting public-book bids 38,709 and 24,900 contracts deep.
- Related, already covered by #60 item 3: the card's "a resting bid to buy it back has been seen on two books, ten contracts each" is the most wrong number on the screen against 38,709. Land both in one commit.

**What changes on screen.** One sentence on the Parlays page.

children.title: Question for Joe: the installed app's login hard-expires 30 days after sign-in - renew on use, and for how long?
children.body:
**Question:** the home-screen app's login hard-expires 30 days after you first sign in, however often you use it. Should the desk renew the session on use (sliding expiry), and if so, how long?

**Terms.** *Session cookie*: the token your browser sends so the desk knows it is you. *Sliding expiry*: every visit pushes the expiry forward, so an app you use daily never logs you out. *Hard expiry*: the clock starts at login and does not move.

**Options**

- **(A) Recommended: sliding 30 days.** Any authenticated request within the window re-issues the cookie for another 30 days. Daily use never expires; 30 days of silence does. Same posture as the Kalshi app itself.
- **(B) Keep the hard 30 days.** You re-enter the token in mid-October and about monthly after. The keychain fills it, so the cost is a tap and a moment of "is this broken?".
- **(C) Sliding 7 days.** Tighter, since this box holds real money and the installed app has its own cookie jar; a week without opening it logs you out.

**Evidence**

- `issueSession` is called only at login; nothing renews it (thirtieth session, tasks/NEXT.md still-open item 2, ADR 0166).
- iOS gives an installed web app its own cookie jar, so the first launch after install asked for the token again on 2026-09-17; that clock runs out around 2026-10-17.
- `/login` is `autoComplete="current-password"`, so re-entry is a keychain fill, not a typed token.

**What changes on screen.** Nothing visible under (A) or (C) except that the login page stops appearing on a schedule; (B) changes nothing and the October login is expected.

children.title: Parlays: print the public-book ask beside the best maker quote, and let Joe ask the makers even when the book has an ask
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** Print the public-book ask beside the best maker quote, and offer "ask the makers anyway" when the book already has an ask.

**Why.** *Line shopping* is buying the same bet at the best of the places that sell it; it is pure profit because the opinion is unchanged. The desk measured on 2026-09-17 that neither surface dominates (the book beat the RFQ on 2 of 3 exits; the RFQ was the only price on the third), and the entry screen still reads one surface: `PriceOnKalshi.tsx:274` mounts `<AskTheMarket>` only when `status === "book_empty"`. The comparison is already half-built and discarded: `_book_ask_tenths` reads the book on every RFQ and stores `book_yes_ask_tenths` (`backend/combo_rfq.py:91-105`), and `_words` reduces it to prose (`:334-340`). The number is fetched and not printed.

**Smallest build.** In `Quotes()`, print the stored book ask beside the best quote: two prices, no subtraction, no verdict (ADR 0071 §2.5's rule for fair-vs-Kalshi). Then mount an "ask the makers anyway" button on the `priced` branch. Asking commits nothing; Joe authorised asking in #59.

**Test.** A rendered-output test that both prices appear when both exist, and that the RFQ button is present on the priced branch.

children.title: Parlays: a maker's quote shows its age, on the surface where three seconds kills it
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** Show the age of a maker's quote, ticking, with the maker window as the threshold.

**Why.** A price without an age cannot be acted on. A combination is a High Volatility Market: the maker stands behind a quote for about 3 seconds and execution follows ~1.1 s behind confirmation (`CONFIRM_WATCH_S` docstring, `backend/combo_rfq.py`; CLAUDE.md "Only `executed` is a fill"). `AskTheMarket.tsx` renders "Best quote: 59.3c" with no timestamp, no age and no expiry; its own docstring says what is on screen is a price that WAS offered. The order-book path two branches away has a ticking `QuoteAge` with a staleness warning (`PriceOnKalshi.tsx:219`, ticket #40) on a surface with a 900 s staleness limit. The 3-second surface has none.

**Smallest build.** Reuse `QuoteAge` against the RFQ's `requested_ms`, threshold from the maker window. One component, already written, mounted in a second place.

**Test.** Rendered-output: the age is present and the stale warning appears past the threshold; mutation: remove the mount and watch it fail.

children.title: Parlays: the Take-it button says what leaves the account, fee included, like Confirm does
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** The Take-it button says what leaves the account, fee included, server-computed, the way Confirm does on the singles ticket.

**Why.** Ticket #39 settled this for the order path in Joe's answer A: the fee goes on the button as an all-in figure, computed by the server, with break-even on the line above (`ManualTicket.tsx:815-835`). `<TakeIt>` in `AskTheMarket.tsx` renders the bare per-contract ask. The combination entry fee is the term this repo measured at ~17 tenths of a cent per contract at 41c and called "the largest term and the only one that ran optimistic" (CLAUDE.md, E3, ADR 0145); `core/hedge.py:combo_entry_fee_tenths` already computes it. Two buttons on one desk that mean different things by the same-looking number is how a bettor's arithmetic drifts. The rule: the number on the button is the number that leaves your account.

**Smallest build.** `/api/parlays/rfq` returns the modelled fee per quote beside `ask_display`; the button renders price + fee, all-in. Fee is the server's, never recomputed in TypeScript (#39's discipline).

**Test.** The route's payload carries the fee; the button's text contains the all-in figure and not the bare ask alone.

Pairs with the size question (dollars on the button) and the quote-age build: all three live inside `<TakeIt>`/`Quotes()` and could ship as one slice.

children.title: Parlays: a combination bought through Take-it is recorded as a position so /hedge can watch it
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** A combination bought through Take-it writes a `parlay_positions` row from the executed quote, so `/hedge` can watch it.

**Why.** `accept_quote_for_joe` (`backend/combo_rfq.py`) writes `combo_rfqs` intent and outcome rows and nothing else. `record_position` has exactly two callers, `routers/hedge.py:73` (hand-typed slip) and `routes.py:4648` (the order path); the RFQ accept is neither. So a combination bought through the newest armed door creates no position, cannot be watched by `/hedge`, and surfaces there through `VenueCoverageBanner` as "1 Kalshi combination at the venue is not recorded here", the desk flagging its own purchase as a mystery. The accept's success copy says the venue's fill is the number to trust and then never shows it.

ADR 0071 makes the record a byproduct, not a target, but the record is what makes closing-line value measurable, and a bet the tool places and does not record can never be scored.

**Smallest build.** On `executed`, call `record_position` with ticker, legs, price and size from the executed quote (the accept already holds them). ADR 0160's `stake_basis` machinery then applies unchanged; this path can set `venue_fill` honestly because the venue's own fill is readable.

**Test.** An executed accept (fake venue) yields one open position with the quote's price; a cancelled or confirmed-only accept yields none. Mutation: drop the call, watch the first fail.

children.title: Parlays: RFQ, maker, quote and shard get glossary entries and a Term wrap on first use
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** Add *RFQ*, *maker*, *quote* and *shard* to the glossary and wrap their first use on the Ask-the-market surface in `<Term>`.

**Why.** The map's standing rule is that every betting term is defined at first use through `frontend/src/lib/glossary.ts` and `<Term>`; 38 terms are wired, and `exchange-shard` exists. `AskTheMarket.tsx` uses RFQ, maker and quote in prose with no `<Term>` anywhere. This is the one screen that spends money in two taps on a mechanism Joe had not met before 2026-09-17. The definition that matters most is *maker*: a private counterparty chose to quote him and may walk away within three seconds, which is what makes "the maker did not confirm" read as normal rather than as a broken tool.

**Smallest build.** Four glossary entries, four `<Term>` wraps. No layout change.

**Test.** The existing glossary-key test (every `<Term k>` resolves) covers the wiring; add the four keys to it.

children.title: Question for Joe: the combinations shard keeps a 10% margin for a fee that is already inside the ask - keep it?
children.body:
**Question:** the desk refuses to ask the makers for more than **90%** of what is on your combinations shard. The reason written next to that number turned out to be wrong. Should the margin stay at 90%, shrink, or go?

**Terms.** *Shard*: Kalshi keeps combination money in its own pot, separate from your singles. *Target*: the dollar amount an RFQ asks for. *Fee-inclusive*: whether the fee comes out of the amount you asked for, or is added on top of it.

## What was believed, and what the record actually says

The margin was added on 2026-09-17 after you hit `insufficient_balance` on a $5 ask against a $3.94 shard. The comment justifying it said Kalshi charges the taker fee **on top of** a fee-inclusive target, so asking for your whole balance would leave nothing to pay the fee with.

Those two halves contradict each other, and this repo's own captured payload settles it. On the real RFQ in `tests/fixtures/combo_rfq_quotes.json`, fired at `target_cost_dollars = "5.0000"`, each maker sized the contracts so that **contracts × ask + fee ≤ $5.00**:

| maker's NO bid | implied YES price | contracts if the fee is inside | contracts if it is not | **what they actually quoted** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.4070 | 59.30c | **8.19** | 8.43 | **8.19** |
| 0.3690 | 63.10c | **7.72** | 7.92 | **7.72** |

Both match the fee-inside column exactly, at the same fee rate this desk already uses. So **the fee is fitted inside your target by the maker**, and asking for your whole shard balance is payable.

That is n = 2 quotes on one request at one size — decisive against the old reason, not a survey of how every maker behaves.

## What it costs you

On a $3.94 shard the desk caps your ask at **$3.55** when $3.94 is payable. That is 10% of your usable combination money, for an argument that does not hold.

**The false sentence is already gone.** The refusal used to tell you "the rest is left for Kalshi's fee, which is charged on top"; it now states the limit and explains nothing, because a screen may not keep saying something the record contradicts. What is left is the number itself, and that is yours.

## Options

- **(A) Recommended: shrink it to 99%.** Keeps a real margin for two small, real things — this desk estimates the fee at 0.071 where the venue charged 0.070, and the maker rounds the contract count down to two decimals — while giving you back essentially all of your shard. Roughly 0.1% held back instead of 10%.
- **(B) Remove it: ask for exactly what you type.** Simplest and matches the evidence. Risk is that a rounding edge sends you back to an `insufficient_balance` refusal after the makers have already answered — which is the failure the margin was invented to stop, and it costs you a wasted ask rather than money.
- **(C) Keep 90%.** Costs a tenth of your shard on every ask, but you never see that refusal.

**What changes on screen.** Only the number in the refusal, and how much you are allowed to type. Nothing else moves.

**Not a brake either way.** ADR 0112's five ceilings stay gone. This is a wall the venue's own balance puts there; the only question is where we stand it.

<sub>Found by a venue review of `b92d6ec` + `523fbda`, 2026-09-18, and re-derived independently from the fixture before the ticket was opened. `backend/combo_rfq.py` `SHARD_HEADROOM`.</sub>

children.title: An RFQ reused at a smaller target reports the target you typed, not the one the venue was asked at
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** `POST /api/parlays/rfq` reports a target the venue may never have been asked at.

**Why.** `create_rfq` (`backend/kalshi/rfq.py`) reuses an existing OPEN RFQ whenever its target is at least the one wanted. `ask_market_to_price` holds RFQs open by default (that is what makes the accept reachable). So: Joe asks at $1.00, then asks again at $5.00 on the same combination, and the second ask reuses the $1.00 RFQ — while the payload reports `target_cost_dollars: "5.0000"`.

He is then shown quotes sized for $1.00 and a field saying $5.00. The Take-it button's all-in figure is computed from the quote's own size, so it stays honest; what lies is the target line and any reading of "you are about to spend about what you typed".

`target_cost_requested` was there to surface exactly this class of divergence, back when an unaffordable target was silently trimmed. The trim is gone (#62), so today the two fields are equal by construction and the real divergence is unreported.

**Smallest build.** Have `create_rfq` return the target it actually used alongside the id, and put that in the payload. Then either render it when it differs, or refuse to reuse an RFQ whose target is below the one asked for — the second is simpler and costs one extra create.

**Test.** Create at $1.00, ask again at $5.00, assert the payload reports the target the venue holds. Mutation: report the requested target unconditionally, watch it fail.

<sub>Venue review of `b92d6ec` + `523fbda`, 2026-09-18.</sub>

children.title: A quote priced finer than a tenth of a cent is dropped, and the screen then says nobody quoted
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** A maker who quotes in hundredths of a cent is dropped, and the screen tells Joe nobody quoted.

**Why.** Combination markets carry `price_level_structure: center_deci_edge_centi_cent` — hundredths of a cent below 1c and above 99c. `_exact_tenths` (`backend/kalshi/rfq.py`) correctly **refuses** such a price rather than rounding it, because rounding would invent a price the venue never offered on the money path. That refusal is right and must stay.

But `parse_quotes` then just `continue`s, and if every quote is refused, `_words` says:

> "Nobody quoted this combination within a few seconds."

Makers did quote. This desk could not represent the price. Those are different facts and the second is actionable — he can go and look in the Kalshi app.

This bites hardest on cheap longshot combinations, which is where the centi-cent region is. The live probe on 2026-09-17 traded at **0.40c**, one tick inside it.

**Smallest build.** Count the refused quotes in `parse_quotes`, carry the count out, and give `_words` a branch: priced, but finer than this desk can represent. The refusal is currently logged and invisible to the reader.

**Test.** A payload whose only quote is `"0.0055"` yields a status and words that do not say nobody quoted. Mutation: fold it back into the empty branch, watch it fail.

<sub>Venue review of `b92d6ec` + `523fbda`, 2026-09-18.</sub>

children.title: Read /portfolio/fills after an executed RFQ accept: it settles partial fills and upgrades the stake to venue_fill
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** After an `executed` RFQ acceptance, read `/portfolio/fills` and record what the venue actually did.

**What it settles, and why it is the highest-value ten lines on this path.**

1. **Partial fills.** ADR 0169 records the position from the quote's own `contracts` and price, on the stated ground that a quote is all-or-nothing at the size asked for. That is **asserted, not measured** — `backend/combo_rfq.py` and `backend/kalshi/rfq.py` both say it, and neither cites a measurement. The only executed accept this repo has was fired at `contracts = 1` on the RFQ, not against a maker's quoted size, and its own measurement doc says in terms: *"Nothing here speaks to slippage, partial fills."* `rest_remainder: False` governs the requester's remainder, not the maker's fill.

   If a quote can part-fill, the recorded position is wrong in both size and stake, `/hedge` sizes a hedge against a holding Joe does not have, and nothing downstream will ever catch it — the stake basis is `as_recorded`, so there is no reconciliation to fail.

2. **`rfq_accept` becomes `venue_fill`.** ADR 0169 added `rfq_accept` precisely because nothing on this path reads what Kalshi charged. `/portfolio/fills` is what ADR 0160 already prefers everywhere else, and it is sitting unread.

3. **It closes ADR 0169's own open question**, which was left unticketed as "a measurement with no decision in it". It has one: what to record.

**Smallest build.** The accept path already polls `read_quote` for up to 10s. On `executed`, one `GET /portfolio/fills?ticker=...` before writing the position; record the venue's count and average price; resolve `stake_basis` to `venue_fill` where the link is provable and keep `rfq_accept` where it is not.

**Test.** A fill payload reporting fewer contracts than quoted produces a position at the venue's size, not the quote's. Mutation: use the quote's size unconditionally, watch it fail.

<sub>Venue review of `b92d6ec` + `523fbda`, 2026-09-18.</sub>

children.title: The shard balance the RFQ wall measures against has no captured payload
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** `read_shard_funds` parses a payload this repo has never captured, and it now gates money.

**Why it matters now.** `backend/store/combo_orders.py` reads `balance_breakdown[i]["balance"]` and does `float(raw) * 1000` on a comment asserting the field is "dollars as a 4dp string". There is **no fixture for `/portfolio/balance`** in `tests/fixtures/`; the only test payload is hand-constructed with an empty `balance_breakdown`, so it exercises none of the parsing.

Kalshi's top-level `balance` is classically an integer in **cents**. If `balance_breakdown[].balance` is cents too, `available_tenths` is **100× high** and the shard wall never fires at all — which is exactly the refusal the wall exists to prevent, arriving at the venue instead, after the makers have answered.

This function predates the change, but `523fbda` promoted it into a money gate on the RFQ path, so it inherits the burden. It is this repo's named failure shape: **a reader for a payload with no fixture** (CLAUDE.md: wire-format tests load captured payloads, never hand-constructed ones).

The 2026-08-30 readings quoted in `backend/kalshi/rest.py` (`21.4120`, `0.0100`) *suggest* dollars. Suggest is not pin.

**Smallest build.** One authenticated `GET /portfolio/balance` captured into `tests/fixtures/`, and a wire-format test over it. Nothing to change if it confirms dollars — which is the good outcome and still worth having written down.

<sub>Venue review of `b92d6ec` + `523fbda`, 2026-09-18.</sub>

children.title: Hedge: show what a combination you hold would sell for, on both surfaces, read-only
children.body:
**Build. The decision is made — #63, Joe's answer (A), 2026-09-18:** show both exit prices on each open combination, read-only, no Sell button. This ticket is the implementation, and it carries one design call he can overturn.

## The blocker nobody had looked at

`parse_quotes` (`backend/kalshi/rfq.py`) requires `no_bid_dollars` and **`continue`s past any quote without one**. A maker bidding only YES — which is exactly what "what would you pay me for this" looks like — is dropped before it reaches anything. `RfqQuote` has no `yes_bid_tenths` field to put it in, and `combo_rfq_quotes` has no column to store it.

So the sell side does not exist yet at any layer. That is the first slice, not a detail.

## The design call, stated so it can be refused

Joe's (A) reads as *both prices, always*. Taken literally on `/hedge` that means firing a real RFQ per open combination on **every build of the page — and `/hedge` is polled.** That is a steady stream of live requests to the exchange for a screen nobody may be looking at, on the surface ADR 0167 had just finished making cheap.

**Taken instead as:**

- the **public-book bid** renders automatically — it is an ordinary Kalshi read, and `OrderBook.best_yes_bid` already exists;
- the **maker bid** sits behind a tap per position ("what would a maker pay for this?"), which is free and commits nothing, exactly as the buy-side ask does.

Still both prices, still read-only, still no Sell button. But it is *not* "both, always", and saying so is the point of this paragraph. If the RFQ should fire automatically, that is a one-line change and Joe's to make.

## What it must not do

- **No Sell button.** Option (C) was not taken. Nothing on `/hedge` may spend.
- **No ranking.** Two prices side by side; neither called the better one. Measured 2026-09-17: the book beat the RFQ on two of three positions and the RFQ was the only exit on the third.
- **No frequency claim in the copy.** #60 and #64 settled that twice.
- **An exit existing is not an exit being good.** Every measured best bid sat below cost basis (7.60 vs 10.20, 4.70 vs 5.70, 0.14 vs 0.38). Show cost basis beside the bids and draw no conclusion.
- **Do not weaken ADR 0078.** Hedging a leg and selling the combination are different actions at different costs. This adds the price of the second; the hedge stays the exit the desk watches.

## Slices

1. `yes_bid_dollars` parsed into `RfqQuote`, stored, and a quote surviving with either side present. Schema bump.
2. The public-book YES bid on each open combination in `/api/hedge`.
3. The per-position ask-the-makers control and its rendering.

<sub>Follows #63 (answered A, closed). Opened 2026-09-18 because a closed ticket carrying a spec belongs to nobody unless it is written down.</sub>

children.title: The RFQ row in the database still says nobody quoted when makers quoted too finely
children.body:
**Build, no decision needed.** The screen now tells the truth and the database still does not.

**Why.** ADR 0172 (#73) gave the RFQ payload a third outcome, `priced_too_finely`: makers answered and every price was finer than a tenth of a cent, so the desk refused it rather than rounding it onto the money path. The screen says so and points at the Kalshi app.

`combo_rfqs.status` does not. `record_quotes` (`backend/store/combo_orders.py`... actually `backend/store/combo_rfqs.py:181-184`) sets the row from the count of quotes it managed to **store**:

```python
(stored, STATUS_QUOTED if stored else STATUS_NO_QUOTES, rfq_id)
```

A refused quote never becomes an `RfqQuote`, so it is not in `seen`, so `stored` is 0, so the durable row reads `no_quotes` — **"we asked and nobody answered"**, which is the exact distinction the constant's own comment says it exists to preserve:

> `quoted` and `no_quotes` are deliberately different rows rather than a count of zero. "We asked and nobody answered" is a measurement about the market; "we asked and never read the answer" is a bug in us.

There is now a third case and it is filed under the first one.

**Why it matters more than the screen did.** The screen is read once. This row is the population any later measurement of *how often a combination goes unquoted* would count, and it is contaminated in the flattering direction — it makes the market look quieter than it is. That is a measurement-rules problem, not a cosmetic one.

**What it costs.** A schema bump. `schema.sql:2726` is `CHECK (status IN ('asked', 'quoted', 'no_quotes', 'error'))` and SQLite cannot widen a CHECK without rebuilding the table, so this is a migration with a `SCHEMA_VERSION` increment — which is why ADR 0172 §3 left it out of #73's "smallest build" rather than folding a migration into a copy fix.

**Smallest build.** Add `priced_too_finely` to the CHECK and to the status constants; thread the refused-id set into `record_quotes` so the row can distinguish "nobody answered" from "we could not represent what they said"; keep `quoted` outranking it, matching the payload's precedence. Consider a `refused_too_fine` column rather than only a status, since a count is the thing a later measurement wants.

**Test.** An RFQ whose only quote is `"0.0055"` writes a row that is not `no_quotes`. Mutation: fold it back, watch it fail. And a migration wind-back test, per the v37/v39 precedent.

<sub>Found while building #73; named in ADR 0172 §3 so it is a known gap rather than a later discovery.</sub>

children.title: Question for Joe: accepting a quote might leave a resting offer on the book - guard it, or accept the risk?
children.body:
**A question only you can answer, and it is about a behaviour you already ruled out once.**

## What was found

Settling #74's measurement half turned up an inference across two of Kalshi's own rules that nobody has looked at:

- **Rule 5.3(b)(e):** when an RFQ quote is accepted, the resulting pair enters the book as ordinary limit orders that *"behave identically to a standard order"*.
- **Rule 5.10(a):** a partially filled standard order **rests on the book at its limit price**.

Chain them and a short-filled RFQ acceptance would leave **a resting offer sitting on the exchange in your name** — the exact behaviour ADR 0115 removed on your word, because you pay the ask and do not make offers. `POST /api/parlays/bid` is disarmed for that reason and has been since 2026-09-08.

## Why this is a question and not a build

**It has never happened.** 11 of 11 executed acceptances in the record filled whole — exactly the quoted size, exactly the quoted price, one fill row each, across quoted sizes from 1.51 to 227.27 contracts (`docs/measurements/2026-09-18-can-an-rfq-quote-partially-fill.md`). So this is not a bug report; nothing has gone wrong.

It is also **not decidable from the documentation**. Kalshi's REST reference, FIX page, RFQ guide, WebSocket schema and Fills schema are all silent on whether an accepted quote can execute short at all. The chain above is an inference across two rulebook paragraphs, never observed, and no read of the existing record can confirm or refute it.

And it cannot be tested without doing the thing in question: you would have to accept a quote large enough to short-fill and watch what the book does afterwards. That spends, and it risks creating the resting offer in order to find out whether resting offers get created.

## The question

**If accepting a maker's quote could leave a resting offer on the book as a side effect — rarely, and never yet observed — does the accept path need a guard, or do you accept the risk?**

Three shapes it could take:

**(a) Accept the risk, change nothing.** It has never happened in 11 of 11, Kalshi's own default on both sides of the `rest_remainder` flag is "do not rest", and a guard against an unobserved event is speculative work on the armed path. The desk's existing `open_orders` visibility would show one if it appeared.

**(b) Read the book after every accept and cancel anything resting.** Turns a one-call accept into accept-then-verify-then-maybe-cancel, with no idempotency key anywhere on that path — and a cancel is another live write. More machinery on the path that spends.

**(c) Check for it once, deliberately, on the next large acceptance you make anyway.** Costs one extra read after a trade you were going to place regardless. Settles it with evidence instead of either accepting or guarding on an inference.

My read is **(c) if you are placing a large one soon, (a) if not** — but the ruling about resting offers is yours and I am not going to infer it from ADR 0115.

## One more thing worth knowing

This is the **second time in two days** that a Kalshi REST page declined to state something its FIX page says outright, on this same endpoint. The first was `accepted_side`, where the wrong reading would have bought the opposite contract at ~250x. The durable rule now recorded: on the RFQ path, read the FIX page before believing the REST reference is complete.

<sub>From #74's measurement half. ADR 0169 Amendment 2 records the same finding and defers it here.</sub>

children.title: Should the parlay builder refuse a leg the singles screen suppresses as a probable bug?
children.body:
**The question:** a leg that the singles screen hides from you as a probable bug is still being multiplied into a parlay card's headline number — should the parlay builder refuse those legs, mark them, or carry on as it does now?

---

### What "suppressed" means here

When the desk works out a fair price for a single market and the answer looks *too good* — a bigger edge than the fee it is hunting — it does not show it. That is rule 1 of this whole project: **a large apparent edge is a bug until proven otherwise**. The row gets a `suppressed_reason` (`suspicious_edge`, `too_few_books`, `no_market_width`) and the screen either hides it or says why it is not trustworthy.

**The parlay path does not do that.** `suppressed_reason` reaches the parlay screen as *display* only: the leg is still selected, still priced, and still multiplied into the card's headline probability. `Recipe` — the object a card is built from — has **no field at all** for book count, suppression, or how old the Kalshi quote was. `min_book_count = 2` exists and feeds only the trust badge.

So one screen calls a number untrustworthy and the other screen quietly multiplies it into a bet.

**Evidence:** `backend/core/ladder.py` builds the pool and `_best_per_game` (`ladder.py:607`) picks legs; the suppression check that the singles path applies is not among the filters. Found while answering "how are parlays chosen?", 2026-09-18 (thirty-fifth session, §5 of that entry).

**Why it matters more on a parlay than on a single.** A parlay multiplies its legs. A leg whose price is wrong by 5 points moves a single bet by 5 points; in a four-leg card it moves the headline by a lot more, and it moves it in the flattering direction, because a suppressed leg is almost always one that looks *too cheap*.

---

### The options

**(a) Refuse a suppressed leg outright** — recommended. The parlay builder drops any leg the singles path would have suppressed, exactly as it already drops a second leg from the same game. Rule 1 applied once, in one place.
*On screen:* fewer cards, and on a thin night possibly none for a given shape. Nothing you see becomes less true; some things stop being offered. The desk would say "no card here tonight" more often.

**(b) Carry the leg but mark the card** — the leg still goes in, and the card carries a visible warning naming the reason ("one leg's price is not trusted: only 2 books"). You decide.
*On screen:* the same cards you get today, with a badge on some of them. Keeps the choice with you, at the cost of putting a number on screen that the rest of the desk says is probably a bug.

**(c) Refuse only `suspicious_edge`, carry the rest** — a split. `suspicious_edge` means "this looks too good", which is the one that flatters a parlay; `too_few_books` and `no_market_width` mean "we could not see enough to say", which is thin evidence rather than a suspicious number.
*On screen:* between (a) and (b). Slightly fewer cards than today, no new badges.

**(d) Leave it exactly as it is.** The parlay screen is for building a bet you were going to make anyway, and you would rather see the card and judge it yourself.
*On screen:* nothing changes. This ticket closes and the contradiction is recorded as a deliberate one rather than an oversight.

---

### What this ticket is not

It is not a proposal to rank parlays by edge — ADR 0071 forbids that and nothing here changes it. It is only about which legs are allowed into a card at all.

Raised under CLAUDE.md workflow step 7 by the 2026-09-18 (thirty-sixth) session; the finding is the previous session's and went unticketed, which is the decay this rule exists to stop.
